pos: v. (to ascend by effort, hand and foot; used of soldiers, of fugitives, and of a flight from God that does not succeed)
etymology: Old English climban, akin to cleave — to go up by clinging. The Hebrew alah is the ordinary verb of going up, the same word used of offering a burnt sacrifice, which goes up in smoke.
biblical_def: Men climb in Scripture for three reasons: to escape, to attack, and to hide from God. To escape: “The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen; they shall go into thickets, and climb up upon the rocks” (Jer 4:29). To attack, in Joel's terrible picture of the locust army that is also an army of men: “They shall run like mighty men; they shall climb the wall like men of war; and they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks” (Joe 2:7), and again, “they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief” (Joe 2:9). And to hide, which is the use that matters most: “Though they dig into hell, thence shall mine hand take them; though they climb up to heaven, thence will I bring them down” (Amo 9:2). Amos piles the impossibilities up — the top of Carmel, the bottom of the sea — and every one of them ends in the same hand. David had already turned the same fact into comfort rather than terror: “If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there” (Psa 139:8). It is the same doctrine; only the man's standing before God differs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to climb as to creep up by little and little, or with labor; to mount or ascend by means of the hands and feet; and figuratively, to rise to a higher condition with effort.
webster_full: CLIMB, v.i. clime. To creep up by little and little, or step by step; to mount or ascend with labor and difficulty.
They shall climb the wall like men of war. Joel ii.
2. To rise or ascend with labor or difficulty; as, to climb to preferment.
CLIMB, v.t. To ascend by means of the hands and feet, implying labor.
scriptures: Joe 2:7
They shall run like mighty men; they shall climb the wall like men of war; and they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks:
Amo 9:2
Though they dig into hell, thence shall mine hand take them; though they climb up to heaven, thence will I bring them down:
If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there.
Jer 4:29
The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen; they shall go into thickets, and climb up upon the rocks: every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein.
corruption_summary: The omnipresence of God is presented almost solely as a comfort, though Amos 9:2 states it first as the reason no man escapes judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 139 is quoted constantly and Amos 9 almost never, yet they assert the same attribute in nearly the same words. God is in heaven and in hell, on Carmel's top and in the sea's bottom; there is no coordinate at which a creature is out of reach. To David this is the ground of a settled peace, because he has said in the same psalm, search me, O God, and know my heart. To the men of Amos's generation the identical truth is the announcement that flight is pointless. Omnipresence is not in itself a comfort; it is a comfort to the reconciled and a terror to the fugitive, and a doctrine of God trimmed to yield only reassurance has stopped being a doctrine of God. Jonah is the narrative proof, since he went down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the sea and down into the fish, and every descent brought him nearer the God he was fleeing.

Joel's climbers give the other application. His army mounts the wall in ranks, every one on his own way, and they do not break their ranks or thrust one another — a discipline more frightening than fury. It is a picture of judgment arriving in good order, and the prophet's response to it is not a strategy but a summons: turn ye even to me with all your heart, and rend your heart, and not your garments. The modern habit is to read every threatening passage as a metaphor for internal difficulty and every promise as a literal guarantee. Joel does the reverse. The locusts and the army are real, the wall really falls, and the mercy offered in the middle of it is real too, for the LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.
roots_summary: Hebrew alah (H5927), to go up, ascend, climb — also the verb behind the burnt offering that goes up; with yarad (H3381), to go down, its constant counterpart.
roots_lines: Hebrew alah (H5927) — to go up, to ascend, to climb; they shall climb the wall like men of war; Joel 2:7.
Hebrew olah (H5930) — a burnt offering, literally that which goes up; from the same root as climb; Leviticus 1:3.
Hebrew yarad (H3381) — to go down; the LORD will bring down those who climb up to heaven; Amos 9:2.
Hebrew sheol (H7585) — the grave, the place of the dead; if I make my bed in hell, thou art there; Psalm 139:8.
Greek anabaino (G305) — to go up, to ascend; Zacchaeus climbed a sycomore tree to see Jesus; Luke 19:4.
usage: “They shall climb the wall like men of war” — judgment arriving in good order.
“Though they climb up to heaven, thence will I bring them down” — the flight that has no destination.
“If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there” — the same truth, and a different man saying it.

pos: v. (to float or move through water; used of iron made to float, of a bed watered with tears, and of a river too deep to cross)
etymology: Old English swimman. The Authorized Version uses it both of a man's stroke through water and, remarkably, of an iron axe head that God made to float.
biblical_def: The most famous use is a miracle about a borrowed tool. A son of the prophets lost an axe head in the Jordan and cried out because it was borrowed; “And the man of God said, Where fell it? And he shewed him the place. And he cut down a stick, and cast it in thither; and the iron did swim” (2Ki 6:6). God attends to a working man's debt over a piece of iron. David uses the word for grief: “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears” (Psa 6:6). Ezekiel is led out into rising water until measurement fails: “it was a river that I could not pass over: for the waters were risen, waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over” (Eze 47:5). Isaiah pictures Moab flailing in his own ruin, spreading forth his hands “as he that swimmeth spreadeth forth his hands to swim” (Isa 25:11). And in the shipwreck at Malta the soldiers plan to kill the prisoners “lest any of them should swim out, and escape” (Act 27:42) — and Paul the prisoner is the reason every soul is spared.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to swim as to float, to be supported on water or other fluid, not to sink; and to move progressively in water by means of the hands and feet.
webster_full: SWIM, v.i. To float; to be supported on water or other fluid; not to sink.
The iron did swim. 2 Kings vi.
2. To move progressively in water by means of the hands and feet, or of fins.
3. To be overflowed or drenched; as, the bed is made to swim with tears.
scriptures: And the man of God said, Where fell it? And he shewed him the place. And he cut down a stick, and cast it in thither; and the iron did swim.
Psa 6:6
I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears.
Eze 47:5
Afterward he measured a thousand; and it was a river that I could not pass over: for the waters were risen, waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over.
And the soldiers' counsel was to kill the prisoners, lest any of them should swim out, and escape.
corruption_summary: The floating axe head is dismissed as a folk tale unworthy of God's attention, though its whole point is that the Lord of heaven concerns Himself with a poor man's borrowed tool.
corruption_paragraphs: Two objections are raised against 2 Kings 6, and they contradict each other. The first is critical: iron does not float, therefore the account is legend, and the miracle stories of Elisha are the folklore of a prophetic school. That objection assumes what it means to prove — if God made the iron, He may make it swim, and the whole question is whether the God of Scripture exists and acts, not whether iron ordinarily floats. The second objection is devotional and more common in churches: the miracle is thought too small, unworthy of divine power, a waste of the supernatural on a piece of hardware. But the text supplies the reason for the man's distress and it is a moral one — for it was borrowed. A poor man had lost what belonged to another and could not repay it. The Lord who counts the hairs of the head and marks the fall of a sparrow acted on precisely that account, and the smallness of the object is the point of the story rather than an embarrassment in it.

Ezekiel's river is the other side of the word, and it corrects a habit of measuring God. The prophet is led out a thousand cubits at a time — to the ankles, to the knees, to the loins — and then to water he cannot pass over. Every stage but the last is measurable, and the vision ends where a man must either swim or turn back. Trees grow on both banks, the desert is healed, the sea itself is made whole; and the one thing a man cannot do is wade through it while keeping his feet. That is a fair picture of the Christian's dealings with God: much can be walked in, understood and taught, and beyond a certain depth there is nothing but committing the whole weight to water that will hold. Psalm 6 shows the same David who wrote that God's ways are past finding out weeping his bed wet all night — and the psalm ends with the LORD having heard the voice of his weeping.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsuph (H6687), to overflow, to float, of the iron; sachah (H7811), to swim, of the stroke and of the tear-soaked bed; Greek ekkolumbao (G1579), to swim out.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsuph (H6687) — to flow over, to make float; and the iron did swim; 2 Kings 6:6.
Hebrew sachah (H7811) — to swim; all the night make I my bed to swim, and Moab spreading his hands; Psalm 6:6, Isaiah 25:11.
Hebrew sachu — waters to swim in, a noun from the same root; Ezekiel 47:5.
Greek ekkolumbao (G1579) — to swim out, to escape by swimming; Acts 27:42.
Greek kolumbao (G2860) — to swim, to dive; those which could swim cast themselves first into the sea; Acts 27:43.
usage: “And the iron did swim” — because it was borrowed.
“All the night make I my bed to swim” — grief measured in a soaked couch.
“Waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over” — the depth past wading.

pos: n. and v. (a marsh reed, the lowliest growth of the water; also to move with violence, as nations rushing)
etymology: Old English risce, a reed of wet ground; and separately, Middle English ruschen, to move violently. The Authorized Version carries both, and Isaiah plays on the first as a figure of the meanest man in Israel.
biblical_def: Bildad opens with a question about the plant: “Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?” (Job 8:11) — the rush is the reed of the marsh, green while the water lasts and withered the moment it fails, and Bildad uses it (wrongly, as applied to Job) as a figure of the hypocrite's hope. Isaiah takes the same plant as the bottom of a society: “Therefore the LORD will cut off from Israel head and tail, branch and rush, in one day” (Isa 9:14), and of Egypt, “Neither shall there be any work for Egypt, which the head or tail, branch or rush, may do” (Isa 19:15). Judgment removes the great and the small together; nobody is beneath it. The verb carries the other sense and one of Isaiah's grandest images: “The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but God shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind” (Isa 17:13). The noise of nations is immense and it is answered by a rebuke.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives rush as a plant of the genus Juncus, growing in wet ground, and proverbially a thing of no value; and to rush as to move forward with impetuosity, violence and tumultuous rapidity.
webster_full: RUSH, n. A plant growing in wet land, of the genus Juncus. Rushes were formerly used for strewing floors.
2. Proverbially, a thing of small value or importance.
RUSH, v.i. To move forward with impetuosity, violence and tumultuous rapidity.
The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters. Isa. xvii.
scriptures: Job 8:11
Can the rush grow up without mire? can the flag grow without water?
Isa 9:14
Therefore the LORD will cut off from Israel head and tail, branch and rush, in one day.

The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but God shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind.
Neither shall there be any work for Egypt, which the head or tail, branch or rush, may do.
corruption_summary: The roar of the nations is mistaken for the decisive power in history, when Isaiah answers the rushing of many waters with a single rebuke.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 17:13 is built to be heard as well as read. The first half is enormous — nations rushing like the rushing of many waters, a sound that fills the world and admits no argument. The second half is one clause: but God shall rebuke them. What follows is not a battle but a scattering; chaff on a mountain before the wind, and a rolling thing before the whirlwind. The corruption to name is the settled modern assumption, shared by the anxious and the triumphant alike, that the loud thing is the real thing. Whole Christian ministries now organise themselves around the noise of the nations, either in dread of it or in the hope of steering it, and the effect in both cases is that the church takes its agenda from the roar. The prophet gives the roar one verse and the rebuke half of one, and the proportion is deliberate.

The plant half of the word is Isaiah's other lesson and it cuts the opposite way. When the LORD cuts off head and tail, branch and rush, the reed is named alongside the palm branch; the mean and the mighty go in one day. This is a standing refutation of the idea that judgment falls on the powerful while the ordinary man is a bystander. It also guards against the reverse sentimentality, common in our own preaching, which treats the poor as innocent by definition. Scripture is tender toward the poor and fierce against those who oppress them, and it never says that being small is being righteous. Bildad's question about the rush is true in itself, however unjustly he aimed it: a reed with no water withers while it is yet green, and any life not rooted in God is exactly that green and exactly that brief.
roots_summary: Hebrew gome (H1573), the papyrus rush of the marshes; agmon (H100), a reed or bulrush, the humble growth of Isaiah's pairs; shaah (H7582), to rush or roar, of the nations.
roots_lines: Hebrew gome (H1573) — papyrus, bulrush; the ark of bulrushes in which Moses was laid; Exodus 2:3, Job 8:11.
Hebrew agmon (H100) — a rush, a reed; branch and rush, the top and bottom of a people; Isaiah 9:14, Isaiah 19:15.
Hebrew shaah (H7582) — to make a rushing noise, to roar; the nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters; Isaiah 17:13.
Hebrew gaar (H1605) — to rebuke; the single word that scatters them; Isaiah 17:13, Psalm 106:9.
Hebrew mots (H4671) — chaff; what the nations become when rebuked; Isaiah 17:13, Psalm 1:4.
usage: “Can the rush grow up without mire?” — green while the water lasts.
“Head and tail, branch and rush, in one day” — the great and the small together.
“But God shall rebuke them” — one clause against the roar of nations.

pos: v. (to clear away with a broom or a flood; used of God's besom of destruction and of a woman seeking a lost coin)
etymology: Old English swapan, to sweep or drive. The Hebrew at Isaiah 14:23 is tuw, to sweep away, joined to matate, a besom — the only place in Scripture where God is pictured with a broom.
biblical_def: Babylon is swept: “I will also make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the LORD of hosts” (Isa 14:23). The figure is domestic and therefore terrible — the city that ruled the world is dust on a floor, and God takes a broom to it. The same prophet turns the picture on the false security of Judah: “Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place” (Isa 28:17). Every word there is a builder's word — line, plummet — and what is measured is a shelter men had built out of falsehood. Then the Lord Jesus takes the same household act and makes it the picture of God's own seeking: “Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?” (Luk 15:8). And when it is found she calls in the neighbours: “Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost” (Luk 15:9). One broom clears a city; another finds a coin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to sweep as to brush or clean with a broom; to carry with a long swinging motion; to drive or carry off a mass of things by a violent force.
webster_full: SWEEP, v.t. To brush or rub over with a brush, broom or besom, for removing loose dirt.
2. To carry with a long swinging motion; as, to sweep the string of an instrument.
3. To drive or carry along or off by a long brushing stroke or force, or by flowing on the earth; as, a river sweeps away a dam.
I will sweep it with the besom of destruction. Isa. xiv.
scriptures: I will also make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water: and I will sweep it with the besom of destruction, saith the LORD of hosts.
Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place.
Luk 15:8
Either what woman having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it?
Luk 15:9
And when she hath found it, she calleth her friends and her neighbours together, saying, Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost.
corruption_summary: The parable of the lost coin is preached as though the coin cooperated, when the whole force of the figure is that silver cannot seek and must be swept for.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 15 gives three parables in ascending order of helplessness, and the middle one is the plainest statement of monergism in the Gospels. A sheep can at least wander back toward a voice; a son can come to himself and rise. A coin lies where it fell. It does not know it is lost, it makes no sound, it cannot signal, and it will lie in the dust of that floor for ever unless a light is lit and the house is swept. Everything in the parable is done by the woman — the candle, the broom, the diligent seeking — and the coin contributes exactly nothing but its own worth to the one who lost it. That is why the parable is so often softened. Preaching that requires the sinner to make the decisive movement has no use for a coin, and quietly reads it as a sheep. The Lord chose three figures on purpose, and He put the passive one in the middle.

The other end of the word keeps the doctrine from being sentimental. The same God who sweeps a floor to find one coin sweeps Babylon with the besom of destruction and hails away the refuge of lies. Isaiah 28 is exact about how that happens: judgment laid to the line and righteousness to the plummet, which is to say the shelter is not knocked down in a rage but measured and found false. Men build refuges of lies in every generation — a covenant with death, the prophet calls it — and they are usually respectable, well-constructed and widely believed. What sweeps them away is not argument but weather sent by God. The mercy in the passage is that Isaiah names the one foundation that hail cannot touch, laid in Zion, a tried stone, a precious corner stone: he that believeth shall not make haste.
roots_summary: Hebrew tuw (H2894), to sweep away, with matate (H4292), a besom or broom; yaah (H3261), to sweep away, of the hail; Greek saroo (G4563), to sweep with a broom.
roots_lines: Hebrew tuw (H2894) — to sweep away; I will sweep it with the besom of destruction; Isaiah 14:23.
Hebrew matate (H4292) — a besom, a broom; used only here in the Old Testament; Isaiah 14:23.
Hebrew yaah (H3261) — to sweep away; the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies; Isaiah 28:17.
Greek saroo (G4563) — to sweep; the woman sweeps the house for the lost piece of silver; Luke 15:8.
Greek drachme (G1406) — a drachma, the piece of silver; a day's wage, and a tenth of her store; Luke 15:8.
usage: “I will sweep it with the besom of destruction” — an empire as dust on a floor.
“The hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies” — measured first, then swept.
“Light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently” — and the coin does nothing.

pos: v. (to rub off the surface; used of a leprous house, of Job's potsherd, and of a city scraped to bare rock)
etymology: Old English scrapian, to scratch or rub. In the law the word belongs to the cleansing of a house; in Job to a man's own body; in Ezekiel to the demolition of a city.
biblical_def: The law provides for a house with a plague in its walls, and the remedy is thorough: “And he shall cause the house to be scraped within round about, and they shall pour out the dust that they scrape off without the city into an unclean place” (Lev 14:41). If the plague returns, the house comes down altogether (Lev 14:45). The infection is not painted over; it is scraped to the stone and the scrapings are carried outside. Job uses the word of himself in his extremity: “And he took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal; and he sat down among the ashes” (Job 2:8) — a man smitten with boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown (Job 2:7), sitting in the ash heap with a piece of broken pot. Ezekiel uses it of Tyre: “they shall destroy the walls of Tyrus, and break down her towers: I will also scrape her dust from her, and make her like the top of a rock” (Eze 26:4). The merchant city becomes bare stone, a place to spread nets on. In all three the word means the same thing: everything down to the bare surface, and no cosmetic remedy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to scrape as to rub the surface of anything with a sharp or hard instrument; to clean by rubbing; to remove by rubbing off the surface.
webster_full: SCRAPE, v.t. To rub the surface of anything with a sharp or hard instrument.
2. To clean by rubbing or scraping; as, to scrape a floor.
3. To remove by rubbing or scraping; usually with off. They shall pour out the dust that they scrape off. Lev. xiv.
4. To collect by laborious effort; as, to scrape together a sum of money.
scriptures: And he shall cause the house to be scraped within round about, and they shall pour out the dust that they scrape off without the city into an unclean place:
Job 2:8
And he took him a potsherd to scrape himself withal; and he sat down among the ashes.
Eze 26:4
And they shall destroy the walls of Tyrus, and break down her towers: I will also scrape her dust from her, and make her like the top of a rock.
Job 42:6
Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.
corruption_summary: Sin is dealt with cosmetically wherever the law's procedure is thought harsh, though Leviticus 14 requires the walls scraped and the dust carried outside the camp.
corruption_paragraphs: The statute of the leprous house is one of the most practical pictures of mortification in Scripture. The priest inspects; the affected stones are taken out and cast into an unclean place outside the city; the house is scraped within round about; the dust is carried out; and if the plague returns, the house is pulled down entire. Nothing about the procedure is quick or convenient, and every step moves the corruption further out rather than deeper in. Set that beside the ordinary way a besetting sin is handled — a resolution, an apology, a resolve to be more careful — and the difference is not one of severity but of realism. What is not scraped out grows back in the wall. Paul's language is the same in temper: mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth, and make not provision for the flesh.

Job's potsherd forbids the opposite error, which is to read every affliction as a plague requiring the scraping of some hidden sin. Job's friends built their case on exactly that assumption and God rebuked them for it by name at the end of the book. Job scraped his boils with a broken piece of pot and sat in ashes, and he had done nothing to earn the boils. What he came to at last was not the discovery of a secret fault but the sight of God: I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes, said after the whirlwind and not before it. And Ezekiel's Tyre is the third use, where the scraping is judgment on a city that said, I am of perfect beauty, and traded in the souls of men. Bare rock is what remains when God removes what a place was proud of, and Tyre's harbour is a place for the spreading of nets to this day.
roots_summary: Hebrew qatsa (H7106), to scrape or cut off, of the leprous house; garad (H1623), to scrape, of Job; sachah (H5500), to scrape away, of Tyre's dust.
roots_lines: Hebrew qatsa (H7106) — to scrape, to cut off; the house scraped within round about; Leviticus 14:41.
Hebrew garad (H1623) — to scrape or scratch; Job took a potsherd to scrape himself; Job 2:8.
Hebrew sachah (H5500) — to scrape or sweep away; I will scrape her dust from her; Ezekiel 26:4.
Hebrew cheres (H2789) — a potsherd, a broken earthen vessel; Job's only instrument; Job 2:8.
Hebrew epher (H665) — ashes; where Job sat, and where he repented at the last; Job 2:8, Job 42:6.
usage: “Scraped within round about” — and the dust carried outside the city.
“A potsherd to scrape himself withal” — affliction that was not a punishment.
“I will also scrape her dust from her” — a merchant city left as bare rock.

pos: n. (a dragnet, the great net drawn along the sea bottom; in Habakkuk, the tackle a conqueror worships)
etymology: From Old English dragan, to draw. The drag of Habakkuk is a fishing implement — the heavy net dragged through the water — and the prophet makes it the idol of an empire.
biblical_def: Habakkuk watches the Chaldean sweep the nations up like fish and describes it in three implements: “They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad” (Hab 1:15). Then comes the sentence that names the sin of every conqueror and every self-made man: “Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous” (Hab 1:16). The empire does not worship a god; it worships its own tackle. And the prophet has already asked what makes it possible: God has made men “as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them” (Hab 1:14). The answer given to Habakkuk's complaint is not an explanation of the Chaldean but a rule for the righteous: “Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith” (Hab 2:4) — the verse Paul takes up three times and Luther after him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives drag as a net drawn along the bottom of the water; also a hook or grapple for drawing under water; and to drag as to pull or haul along the ground by main force.
webster_full: DRAG, v.t. To pull; to haul; to draw along the ground by main force.
2. To draw along slowly or heavily; to draw any thing burdensome.
DRAG, n. A net drawn along the bottom of the water.
They burn incense unto their drag. Hab. i.
scriptures: Hab 1:15
They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad.
Hab 1:16
Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous.
Hab 1:14
And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them?
Hab 2:4
Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as bowing to a carved figure, when Habakkuk's conqueror burns incense to the instrument of his own success and never leaves the harbour.
corruption_paragraphs: Habakkuk 1:16 is the sharpest definition of practical idolatry in the prophets, and it involves no image at all. The Chaldean sacrifices to his net. He has looked at the machinery by which he prospered — his army, his method, his fleet — and concluded that it is what fed him, and so his devotion goes there. The tell is given in the same verse: because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous. Whatever a man credits for his fatness gets his incense. In our own setting the drag is a business, a portfolio, a platform, a network of the right relationships, or a method of ministry; and the worship is not usually spoken. It shows in what a man will not risk, what he defends most fiercely, and what he assumes he cannot live without. Deuteronomy warned Israel against the identical sentence before they ever crossed Jordan: thou say in thine heart, My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth.

The prophet's complaint in verse 14 is worth stating carefully because it is often quoted as though Scripture agreed with it. Habakkuk protests that God has made men as the fishes of the sea… that have no ruler over them — that is his charge, brought in prayer, and the whole book is God's answer to it. The answer does not deny the Chaldean's violence or excuse it; chapter two pronounces five woes on him. What it does is refuse to let the righteous man live by his reading of the times. The just shall live by his faith is given in the middle of an unanswered question, and Habakkuk ends singing that though the fig tree shall not blossom and there be no herd in the stalls, yet will he rejoice in the LORD. That is what a man has when his drag is empty, and it is the only thing worth having when it is full.
roots_summary: Hebrew mikmereth (H4365), a fishing net or drag; cherem (H2764), a net; with zabach (H2076), to sacrifice, and qatar (H6999), to burn incense — both given to tackle.
roots_lines: Hebrew mikmereth (H4365) — a drag net; they burn incense unto their drag; Habakkuk 1:16.
Hebrew cherem (H2764) — a net; also, by a separate root, a devoted thing; Habakkuk 1:15.
Hebrew zabach (H2076) — to slaughter, to sacrifice; offered here to a fishing net; Habakkuk 1:16.
Hebrew emunah (H530) — steadfastness, faithfulness, faith; the just shall live by his faith; Habakkuk 2:4.
Greek sagene (G4522) — a dragnet; the kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea; Matthew 13:47.
usage: “They gather them in their drag” — nations taken like fish.
“They sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag” — idolatry with no image.
“The just shall live by his faith” — the answer given while the question stood.

pos: v. (to strike the hands together; in Scripture both a shout of homage and a gesture of scorn)
etymology: Old English clappan, to beat or throb. The Hebrew taqa is to strike or drive, used of clapping hands and of blowing a trumpet — a percussive act.
biblical_def: The same gesture means opposite things in Scripture, and the difference is the object. Homage: “O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph” (Psa 47:1), a psalm that goes on to say why — “For the LORD most high is terrible; he is a great King over all the earth” (Psa 47:2). Creation joins in: “Let the floods clap their hands: let the hills be joyful together” (Psa 98:8), and again, “all the trees of the field shall clap their hands” (Isa 55:12). Scorn: “Men shall clap their hands at him, and shall hiss him out of his place” (Job 27:23), and over the ruined city, “All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth?” (Lam 2:15). The hands are the same; the heart behind them is not. Applause in Scripture is never neutral — it is either the acclamation of a King or the derision of the fallen.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to clap as to strike with a quick motion, to bring two things together suddenly with noise; and specifically, to applaud by striking the hands together.
webster_full: CLAP, v.t. To strike with a quick motion, so as to make a noise by the collision; to strike with something broad, or having a flat surface.
2. To thrust; to drive together; to shut hastily; as, to clap a door.
3. To applaud; to manifest approbation by striking the hands together.
O clap your hands, all ye people. Ps. xlvii.
scriptures: Psa 47:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm for the sons of Korah. O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph.
For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.
Lam 2:15
All that pass by clap their hands at thee; they hiss and wag their head at the daughter of Jerusalem, saying, Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty, The joy of the whole earth?
Men shall clap their hands at him, and shall hiss him out of his place.
corruption_summary: Applause in the assembly is defended by Psalm 47 and attacked by nothing at all, when the question Scripture actually asks is who is being acclaimed.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 47 does command clapping, and it is honest to say so; the objection that any bodily expression in worship is fleshly cannot be sustained from a Bible in which hands are lifted, knees are bowed and the floods are told to clap. But the psalm attaches the gesture to a definite object and a stated reason. Clap your hands, all ye people — and then, for the LORD most high is terrible; he is a great King over all the earth. It is homage rendered to a King at His ascension, the same acclamation a returning conqueror received at the gate. That is a different thing from applause given to performers at the front of a room, and the difference is not fussiness. Where a congregation applauds a singer, a speaker or itself, the form of Psalm 47 has been kept and its object exchanged; and the regulative principle exists precisely to ask, of every element in worship, what God has appointed and to whom it is directed.

Lamentations supplies the other clapping and it should be read whenever the first is quoted. Men clap at ruined Jerusalem, hiss, and wag the head, and repeat her old titles back at her as a taunt — Is this the city that men call The perfection of beauty? Applause of that kind is alive and well in every generation, and Christians are not immune to enjoying it when a fallen minister or a rival congregation supplies the occasion. Job's friend describes the same scene as the fate of the wicked, and the book's ending makes clear how badly a man may misapply that description to his suffering neighbour. Isaiah 55 is the promise that ends the matter: the day comes when the trees of the field clap their hands, and the thorn is replaced by the fir tree, for a name unto the LORD that shall not be cut off.
roots_summary: Hebrew taqa (H8628), to strike or clap; machaa (H4222), to clap or smite the hands, of floods and trees; saphaq (H5606), to clap in derision.
roots_lines: Hebrew taqa (H8628) — to strike, to clap, to blow a trumpet; O clap your hands, all ye people; Psalm 47:1.
Hebrew machaa (H4222) — to strike the hands together; let the floods clap their hands; Psalm 98:8, Isaiah 55:12.
Hebrew saphaq (H5606) — to clap, often in mockery or grief; men shall clap their hands at him; Job 27:23.
Hebrew sharaq (H8319) — to hiss, to whistle; the companion gesture of derision; Lamentations 2:15.
Hebrew teruah (H8643) — a shout, a blast; the voice of triumph in the same verse as the clapping; Psalm 47:1.
usage: “O clap your hands, all ye people” — homage to an ascending King.
“All the trees of the field shall clap their hands” — creation at the restoration.
“All that pass by clap their hands at thee” — the same gesture, turned to scorn.

pos: v. (moved in measured steps; in Scripture both the king's worship and the harlot's snare)
etymology: Old French dancier. The Hebrew karar at 2 Samuel 6 means to whirl about; the Greek orcheomai is the ordinary word for dancing, used of Herodias' daughter and in the Lord's parable of the children in the marketplace.
biblical_def: Two dances stand at the extremes of Scripture. David's: “And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod” (2Sa 6:14). His wife watched and “saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart” (2Sa 6:16), and David's answer was that he would yet be more vile than that. The dance was before the LORD, in a priestly garment, at the return of the ark. The other: “when Herod's birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod” (Mat 14:6); Mark adds that “the king said unto the damsel, Ask of me whatsoever thou wilt” (Mar 6:22), and a prophet's head was carried in on a charger. Before them, and to please a man — the whole difference is in the two prepositions. Israel had a dance of victory when Miriam took a timbrel and the women followed (Exo 15:20), and the Preacher grants “a time to dance” (Ecc 3:4). Benjamin's wives were seized out of a dance at Shiloh (Jdg 21:23), which the book records without approving. And the Lord's own complaint against His generation was that it would neither dance nor lament (Mat 11:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to dance as to leap or step with measured steps, regulated by music; and notes that the ancient sacred dances were performed in worship, distinct from those of festivity.
webster_full: DANCE, v.i. To leap or step with measured steps, regulated by a tune, sung or played on a musical instrument.
2. To leap and frisk about; to move nimbly or up and down.
DANCE, v.t. To make to dance; to dandle, as an infant.
David danced before the Lord with all his might. 2 Sam. vi.
scriptures: And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod.
And as the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart.
Mat 14:6
But when Herod's birthday was kept, the daughter of Herodias danced before them, and pleased Herod.
Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
corruption_summary: David's dance is used to license whatever a worshipper feels moved to do, and Michal's contempt to silence every objection, though the text specifies both the object and the garment.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Samuel 6 is quoted as the charter of unrestrained expression in worship, and the details of the chapter are usually left out. David danced before the LORD — the object is named — and he was girded with a linen ephod, a priestly garment, at the appointed return of the ark to its place. He was not improvising a private ecstasy; he was leading a procession that the earlier part of the same chapter shows him getting badly wrong the first time, when Uzzah died because the ark was carried on a cart instead of on the shoulders of Levites as the law required. The chapter is therefore an unlikely proof text for the view that God accepts any worship offered with sincerity, since it contains one of Scripture's starkest lessons that He does not. Michal's sin was real and is named, but her presence in the chapter does not turn every question about worship into contempt.

The second dance settles the matter from the other side, and it is not settled by squeamishness. Herodias' daughter danced before them, and the text says plainly that she pleased Herod — a girl used by her mother as a lever, a drunken oath sworn before guests, and John the Baptist beheaded in a prison because a king would not lose face. Nothing in Scripture forbids dancing as such; the Preacher grants a time for it, Miriam led one, and the father in the Lord's parable had music and dancing in the house when his son came home. What Scripture does is ask the two questions this word always raises: before whom, and to please whom. Where the answer is God, the ephod is on and the king may be as vile as David was willing to be. Where the answer is a room of men, the end of it is a charger.
roots_summary: Hebrew karar (H3769), to whirl, of David; machowl (H4234), a dance, of Miriam and the daughters of Shiloh; Greek orcheomai (G3738), to dance.
roots_lines: Hebrew karar (H3769) — to whirl, to dance; David danced before the LORD with all his might; 2 Samuel 6:14.
Hebrew machowl (H4234) — a round dance; praise him with the timbrel and dance; Psalm 150:4, Exodus 15:20.
Hebrew ephod bad — a linen ephod, the priestly garment David wore in the procession; 2 Samuel 6:14.
Greek orcheomai (G3738) — to dance; the daughter of Herodias, and the children in the marketplace; Matthew 14:6, Matthew 11:17.
Greek choros (G5525) — a band of dancers, dancing; heard by the elder brother from the field; Luke 15:25.
usage: “David danced before the LORD with all his might” — the object named, and the ephod on.
“She despised him in her heart” — and David said he would be yet more vile.
“Danced before them, and pleased Herod” — the other preposition, and its price.

pos: v. (caught sight of, discovered by looking; used of Moses, of the spies at Jericho, of a watchman, and of a burial party)
etymology: Old French espier, to watch. In the Authorized Version the word usually means simply to catch sight of, though it keeps its stronger sense in the men who spied out the land.
biblical_def: Four scenes, and each turns on what a man saw. Moses: “when Moses was grown… he went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens: and he spied an Egyptian smiting an Hebrew, one of his brethren” (Exo 2:11) — and then, “he looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he slew the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand” (Exo 2:12). Right indignation, taken into his own hands, forty years in Midian. Jericho: “But Joshua had said unto the two men that had spied out the country, Go into the harlot's house, and bring out thence the woman, and all that she hath, as ye sware unto her” (Jos 6:22) — and Hebrews says Rahab perished not with them that believed not, “when she had received the spies with peace” (Heb 11:31). A watchman: “And there stood a watchman on the tower in Jezreel, and he spied the company of Jehu as he came” (2Ki 9:17). And a burial interrupted: “as they were burying a man, that, behold, they spied a band of men; and they cast the man into the sepulchre of Elisha: and when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet” (2Ki 13:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to spy as to see, to gain sight of, to discover at a distance or in a state of concealment; and secondly, to search or discover by close search or examination.
webster_full: SPY, v.t. To see; to gain sight of; to discover at a distance, or in a state of concealment.
He spied an Egyptian smiting an Hebrew. Ex. ii.
2. To discover by close search or examination.
3. To explore; to view, inspect and examine secretly; as a country. Josh. vi.
scriptures: Exo 2:11
And it came to pass in those days, when Moses was grown, that he went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens: and he spied an Egyptian smiting an Hebrew, one of his brethren.
Exo 2:12
And he looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no man, he slew the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand.
Jos 6:22
But Joshua had said unto the two men that had spied out the country, Go into the harlot's house, and bring out thence the woman, and all that she hath, as ye sware unto her.

And it came to pass, as they were burying a man, that, behold, they spied a band of men; and they cast the man into the sepulchre of Elisha: and when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.
corruption_summary: Moses at the Egyptian is preached as a model of standing up for the oppressed, when the text records a right cause taken into a man's own hand and buried in the sand.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 2 is a favourite text for a certain kind of activism, and half of it supports the use. Moses went out to his brethren, looked on their burdens, and saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew; Hebrews 11 commends him for refusing to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter and choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God. So far the sympathy is right and the cost is real. What follows is the part that is dropped: he looked this way and that way, saw that there was no man, killed the Egyptian and hid the body in the sand. The looking about is the giveaway — the act needed darkness. And it accomplished nothing; the next day two Hebrews threw it back at him, and Moses fled. Forty years later God delivered Israel by the same man, on the same errand, and the difference was not that his indignation had cooled but that he went with a commission, a word, and a rod. Righteous anger without a mandate buries its work in the sand.

The other two scenes are pure mercy and are worth setting beside it. The men who had spied out the country were sent back into a city under judgment for one purpose: to bring out a harlot and all her household, because they had sworn to her. Rahab is in the genealogy of Christ, and Hebrews puts her among the faithful. And in 2 Kings 13 a burial party, hurrying because they spied a band of raiders, threw a corpse into Elisha's tomb, and the dead man rose when he touched the prophet's bones. Nothing in that scene is planned by anyone; the mourners were interrupted, the burial was undignified, and God gave a resurrection anyway. Both accounts say the same thing about what a man catches sight of: the sight that matters most is often not the one he was looking for.
roots_summary: Hebrew raah (H7200), to see; ragal (H7270), to go about on foot, hence to spy out a land; tsaphah (H6822), to watch as a watchman.
roots_lines: Hebrew raah (H7200) — to see, to look upon; he spied an Egyptian smiting an Hebrew; Exodus 2:11.
Hebrew ragal (H7270) — to go on foot, to spy out; the two men that had spied out the country; Joshua 6:22.
Hebrew tsaphah (H6822) — to look out, to keep watch; the watchman on the tower in Jezreel; 2 Kings 9:17.
Hebrew chaphar (H2658) — to search out, to explore; the twelve sent to search the land; Deuteronomy 1:22.
Greek kataskopos (G2685) — a spy; Rahab received the spies with peace; Hebrews 11:31.
usage: “He spied an Egyptian smiting an Hebrew” — a right cause, and no commission.
“The two men that had spied out the country” — sent back to keep an oath to a harlot.
“They spied a band of men” — an interrupted burial, and a resurrection nobody planned.

pos: v. (to lay hold of by force; used of a city taken, of death laying hold, and of an inheritance men meant to steal)
etymology: Old French seisir, to put in possession. The legal sense — to be seised of an estate — stands behind the parable's use, where the husbandmen intend to possess the vineyard by killing the heir.
biblical_def: Joshua uses the word at Ai, and joins it to a promise: “Then ye shall rise up from the ambush, and seize upon the city: for the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand” (Jos 8:7). Men lay hold, and God delivers; the sentence contains both without apology. The psalmist prays it against the wicked: “Let death seize upon them, and let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them” (Psa 55:15). But the decisive use is in the Lord's own parable of the vineyard, where the tenants see the owner's son: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance” (Mat 21:38). They knew who He was — that is the point of the sentence — and killed Him for the estate. The next verse is the crucifixion in miniature: “And they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him” (Mat 21:39), outside the city, as Hebrews says of Christ suffering without the gate. Seizing an inheritance is the oldest form of rebellion: to have the Father's things without the Father's Son.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to seize as to fall or rush upon suddenly and lay hold on; to gripe or grasp suddenly; and in law, to take possession of, as of an estate.
webster_full: SEIZE, v.t. To fall or rush upon suddenly and lay hold on; to gripe or grasp suddenly.
2. To take possession by force, with or without right.
3. To invade suddenly; to take sudden hold of; as, a fever seizes a patient.
Let us seize on his inheritance. Matt. xxi.
scriptures: Jos 8:7
Then ye shall rise up from the ambush, and seize upon the city: for the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand.
But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance.
And they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him.
Let death seize upon them, and let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them.
corruption_summary: The husbandmen are read as men who mistook the son, when the Lord has them recognise Him first — this is the heir — and kill Him because of it.
corruption_paragraphs: A comfortable reading of the parable makes the tenants ignorant: they did not know who He was, and if they had, they would not have done it. The Lord Jesus forecloses that reading in the tenants' own words. This is the heir; come, let us kill him. Recognition is the motive, not the missing element. That matters for how unbelief is understood. Scripture does not present the rejection of Christ as a failure of information which better evidence would have cured; it presents it as a rebellion of the will against a rightful owner, sharpened rather than softened by knowing whose vineyard it is. Romans says the same of the heathen who knew God and glorified Him not as God. The one thing the tenants would not have was a landlord, and the one thing the natural heart will not have is a Lord.

The word carries a further sting in its legal sense. To be seised of an estate is to hold it lawfully; the husbandmen wanted the standing of heirs without the relation of sons, and thought a murder could supply it. That is a fair description of every religion of works, in which a man means to hold the Father's inheritance on the ground of his own tenancy — his labour in the vineyard, his fruit, his long occupancy — rather than by union with the Son. The gospel answers it exactly: the inheritance is not seized, it is received, and it is received only in Christ, joint-heirs with Him. Joshua 8 sets the honest use of the word beside the wicked one. Israel was told to seize a city, and told in the same breath that the LORD would deliver it into their hand; the taking was real, the giving was prior, and no man at Ai supposed the city was his by right of arms.
roots_summary: Hebrew yarash (H3423), to take possession, to dispossess; nashah (H5378), to lay hold of, at Psalm 55:15; Greek katecho (G2722), to hold fast, and krateo (G2902), to seize.
roots_lines: Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to seize, to possess, to inherit; seize upon the city, for the LORD will deliver it; Joshua 8:7.
Hebrew nashah (H5378) — to lay hold of; let death seize upon them; Psalm 55:15.
Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold down, to possess; let us seize on his inheritance; Matthew 21:38.
Greek krateo (G2902) — to lay hold of by force; they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard; Matthew 21:39.
Greek kleronomia (G2817) — an inheritance; received by sons in Christ, never seized; Romans 8:17, Ephesians 1:11.
usage: “Seize upon the city: for the LORD your God will deliver it” — the taking real, the giving prior.
“This is the heir… let us seize on his inheritance” — recognition as the motive.
“They caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him” — the cross in a sentence.
